authoredSolutions.1: The stone leaves the balloon with the balloon's own velocity, so it is projected upward with \(u=10\ \text{m/s}\) from a height \(h=75\ \text{m}\). Taking upward as positive and \(g=10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\), \[-75=10t-\tfrac{1}{2}(10)t^{2}\] which gives \(t^{2}-2t-15=0\), so \((t-5)(t+3)=0\) and \(t=5\ \text{s}\). During this time the balloon, moving at constant speed, rises a further \(10\times 5=50\ \text{m}\). Height of the balloon above the ground \[=75+50=125\ \text{m}.\]
authoredSolutions.2: The argument of a trigonometric function must be dimensionless, so \([Bx]=1\) gives \([B]=L^{-1}\) and \([Dt]=1\) gives \([D]=T^{-1}\). Since \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) are themselves dimensionless, \(A\) and \(C\) must carry the dimensions of force, \([A]=[C]=MLT^{-2}\). Therefore \[\left[\frac{AD}{B}\right]=\frac{\left(MLT^{-2}\right)\left(T^{-1}\right)}{L^{-1}}=ML^{2}T^{-3}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.3: Starting from rest, \[v=\int_{0}^{t}\left(\alpha t+\beta t^{2}\right)dt=\frac{\alpha t^{2}}{2}+\frac{\beta t^{3}}{3}.\] The displacement between \(t=1\) and \(t=2\) is \[\Delta x=\int_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{\alpha t^{2}}{2}+\frac{\beta t^{3}}{3}\right)dt=\left[\frac{\alpha t^{3}}{6}+\frac{\beta t^{4}}{12}\right]_{1}^{2}=\frac{7\alpha}{6}+\frac{15\beta}{12}=\frac{7\alpha}{6}+\frac{5\beta}{4}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.4: Equal de Broglie wavelengths mean equal momenta, \(p=h/\lambda\), for both particles. For the electron (non-relativistic) \[K_{e}=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}=\frac{pv}{2},\] since \(p=mv\). For the photon the whole energy is kinetic, \[K_{ph}=pc=pC.\] Hence \[\frac{K_{e}}{K_{ph}}=\frac{pv/2}{pC}=\frac{v}{2C}.\] The matching option is C.
authoredSolutions.5: For a soap bubble the excess pressure is \(P=\dfrac{4T}{R}\) and the enclosed volume is \(V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\). An isothermal combination conserves \(PV\) for the trapped air: \[PV=P_{1}V_{1}+P_{2}V_{2}\] \[\frac{4T}{R}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=\frac{4T}{R_{1}}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi R_{1}^{3}+\frac{4T}{R_{2}}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi R_{2}^{3}\] \[R^{2}=R_{1}^{2}+R_{2}^{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad R=\sqrt{R_{1}^{2}+R_{2}^{2}}.\] The matching option is D.
authoredSolutions.6: Torque on a dipole is \(\tau=pB\sin\theta\). The first dipole is at \(37^{\circ}\) to the field, so \[\tau_{1}=p_{1}B\sin 37^{\circ}=\frac{3}{5}p_{1}B.\] The second dipole is perpendicular to the first, hence at \(127^{\circ}\) to the field, and \[\tau_{2}=p_{2}B\sin\left(90^{\circ}+37^{\circ}\right)=p_{2}B\cos 37^{\circ}=\frac{4}{5}p_{2}B.\] Setting \(\tau_{1}=\tau_{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{3}{5}p_{1}=\dfrac{4}{5}p_{2}\), so \[\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\frac{4}{3}.\] The matching option is A.
authoredSolutions.7: Let \(|\vec{X}|=|\vec{Y}|=A\) and let \(\theta\) be the angle between them. Squaring \(|\vec{X}-\vec{Y}|=10\,|\vec{X}+\vec{Y}|\), \[2A^{2}\left(1-\cos\theta\right)=100\cdot 2A^{2}\left(1+\cos\theta\right)\] \[1-\cos\theta=100+100\cos\theta\] \[101\cos\theta=-99\quad\Rightarrow\quad\cos\theta=-\frac{99}{101}.\] Hence \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{99}{101}\right)\), the matching option being B.
authoredSolutions.8: Initial angular speed \[\omega_{0}=200\ \text{rpm}=200\times\frac{2\pi}{60}=\frac{20\pi}{3}\ \text{rad/s}.\] Stopping uniformly in \(t=10\ \text{s}\), \[\alpha=\frac{\omega_{0}}{t}=\frac{20\pi}{30}=\frac{2\pi}{3}\ \text{rad/s}^{2}.\] For a disc, \(I=\dfrac{MR^{2}}{2}=\dfrac{M(2)^{2}}{2}=2M\). Therefore \[\tau=I\alpha=2M\times\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi M}{3}.\] The matching option is A.
authoredSolutions.9: Each side of the square carries \(\dfrac{16}{4}=4\ \Omega\). The cell sits across side \(AB\), so that \(4\ \Omega\) side is in parallel with the remaining three sides in series, \(12\ \Omega\): \[R_{ext}=\frac{4\times 12}{4+12}=3\ \Omega.\] With the internal resistance, \[I=\frac{\varepsilon}{R_{ext}+r}=\frac{9}{3+1}=\frac{9}{4}\ \text{A}.\] The potential difference across the square network is the terminal voltage \[V=\varepsilon-Ir=9-\frac{9}{4}(1)=6.75\ \text{V}.\] The matching option is C.
authoredSolutions.10: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically, so \(r_{1}=r_{2}=A/2\) and \(i=\dfrac{A+\delta_{\min}}{2}\). Snell's law at the first face then gives \[\mu=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r_{1}}=\frac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A+\delta_{\min}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.11: The undecayed fraction after \(n\) half-lives is \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}\). Here \[\frac{1}{8}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=3.\] Three half-lives occupy 30 years, so \[T_{1/2}=\frac{30}{3}=10\ \text{years}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.12: The modulation index is \[\mu=\frac{A_{m}}{A_{c}}=\frac{20}{20}=1,\] that is \(100\%\). The matching option is D.
authoredSolutions.13: For a charge moving perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), \[r=\frac{mv}{qB}.\] With equal charges and the same field, \(r\propto mv\), so \[\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}\cdot\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{3}{2}=\frac{3}{4}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.14: Einstein's equation gives \[4.8=\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi,\qquad 1.6=\frac{hc}{2\lambda}-\phi.\] From the first, \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=4.8+\phi\); substituting into the second, \[1.6=\frac{4.8+\phi}{2}-\phi\quad\Rightarrow\quad 3.2=4.8-\phi\quad\Rightarrow\quad\phi=1.6\ \text{eV}.\] The threshold wavelength is \[\lambda_{0}=\frac{1240\ \text{eV nm}}{1.6\ \text{eV}}=775\ \text{nm}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.15: For an ideal heat engine \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_{s}}{T_{h}}\). Initially \[\frac{1}{6}=1-\frac{T_{s}}{T_{h}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{T_{s}}{T_{h}}=\frac{5}{6}.\] Lowering the sink by \(62\) degrees doubles the efficiency: \[\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{T_{s}-62}{T_{h}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{T_{s}-62}{T_{h}}=\frac{2}{3}.\] Subtracting, \[\frac{62}{T_{h}}=\frac{5}{6}-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{6}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{h}=372\ \text{K}.\]
authoredSolutions.16: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, \(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB\), so \[r=\frac{mv}{qB}.\] With equal masses and the same field, \[\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}=\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}\cdot\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}=\frac{V}{2V}\times\frac{Q}{2Q}=\frac{1}{4}.\] The matching option is C.
authoredSolutions.17: The force is along \(\hat{j}\) and the displacement is along \(y\), so \[W=\int_{0}^{2}(5y+4)\,dy=\left[\frac{5y^{2}}{2}+4y\right]_{0}^{2}=10+8=18\ \text{J}.\] The matching option is B.
authoredSolutions.18: Measure time from the instant the current is maximum, so \(i=i_{0}\cos\omega t\). The current equals its rms value when \[\frac{i_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}=i_{0}\cos\omega t\quad\Rightarrow\quad\omega t=\frac{\pi}{4}.\] Hence \[t=\frac{\pi/4}{2\pi f}=\frac{1}{8f}=\frac{1}{8\times 50}=2.5\times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}=2.5\ \text{ms}.\] The matching option is A. The values of resistance and voltage are not needed.
authoredSolutions.19: From the figure the first circuit is \(20\ \text{V}\) across \(R=5\ \Omega\), so \[P_{1}=\frac{V^{2}}{R}=\frac{400}{5}=80\ \text{W}.\] The second is a series \(RLC\) circuit with \(R=5\ \Omega\), \(L=0.1\ \text{H}\), \(C=40\ \mu\text{F}\) on a \(20\ \text{V}\) source, whose average power is \[P_{2}=\frac{V^{2}R}{Z^{2}}=\frac{400\times 5}{Z^{2}}.\] Equating the two powers gives \(Z^{2}=25\), i.e. \(Z=R=5\ \Omega\), which is the resonance condition \(X_{L}=X_{C}\). Therefore \[\omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.1\times 40\times 10^{-6}}}=\frac{1}{2\times 10^{-3}}=500\ \text{rad/s}.\] The matching option is B.

authoredSolutions.50: The circulant determinant equals \((\sin x-\cos x)^2(\sin x+2\cos x)\). On \([-\tfrac\pi4,\tfrac\pi4]\), \(\sin x=\cos x\) only at \(x=\tfrac\pi4\), while \(\tan x=-2\) has no solution there — so there is exactly \(1\) solution.
authoredSolutions.52: \(\operatorname{Re}(z^2)+2(\operatorname{Im}z)^2+2\operatorname{Re}(z)=x^2-y^2+2y^2+2x=x^2+y^2+2x=0\): a circle with centre \((-1,0)\). The parabola \(x^2-6x+y+13=0\) has vertex \((3,-4)\). The line through \((-1,0)\) and \((3,-4)\) has slope \(-1\), i.e. \(y=-x-1\), giving \(y\)-intercept \(-1\).

authoredSolutions.55: For even \(n\), \(\big[\tfrac n2\big]=\tfrac n2\); for odd \(n\), \(\big[-\tfrac n2\big]=-\tfrac{n+1}2\). Summing \(n=8\) to \(100\): the even part is \(4+5+\cdots+50=1269\) and the odd part is \(-(5+6+\cdots+50)=-1265\), giving a total of \(4\).
authoredSolutions.57: The general term \(\binom{12}{k}2^{(12-k)/3}3^{k/4}\) is rational iff \(3\mid(12-k)\) and \(4\mid k\), i.e. \(k\in\{0,12\}\): \(2\) rational terms. Of the \(13\) terms, \(11\) are irrational.
